item.title: A2 · Who Pays the Price? Rising Rents and Low- and Middle-Income Households
item.description:
1. The load sits at the bottom. Eurostat's 2025 figures show 11.2 percent of people in Germany living in households that spend more than 40 percent of disposable income on housing, against 7.7 percent in the EU. In the poorest income fifth the share is 31.5 percent, in the second fifth 12.1 (EU: 7.1), in the middle fifth 7.0 (EU: 3.3), and in the top two fifths 3.8 and 1.5. This overburden rate counts total housing costs, including heating and utilities, after housing benefit is deducted, so it is not last episode's rent burden. On average, people living alone put 33.2 percent of disposable income into housing costs and single parents 31.7, against 21.3 for two adults without children; Destatis warns that the 2020 survey change rules out comparison with earlier years and the 2023 change in the owner questions limits it.
2. What is left after rent. Andrej Holm's team at Humboldt University used the 2018 Mikrozensus, the household survey, for 77 large cities and measured the income left after rent including utilities and heating. Households below the poverty threshold, under 60 percent of the median income, had on average 506 euros a month left; households above 140 percent of the median had 3,372 euros. Of households at 60 to 80 percent of the median, 69.8 percent paid more than 30 percent of their income, as did 63.5 percent of single parents and 62.1 percent of people living alone. Of the more than a million households left below the basic benefit rate, about 450,000 live on transfers alone and about 630,000 have earnings of their own.
3. Savings and wealth. The economists Christian Dustmann, Bernd Fitzenberger and Markus Zimmermann followed household budgets from 1993 to 2013. In the poorest fifth, housing's share of income rose from 27 to 39 percent, the average savings rate fell from 2 percent to minus 1 percent, and the share with any positive savings fell from 64 to 53 percent. Their sample includes owners. Median net wealth is 16,200 euros for renter households and 364,800 euros for owner-occupiers, according to the Bundesbank, which says age, household size and income explain part of the gap. Markus Grabka and Christoph Halbmeier of DIW Berlin add that a mortgage forces owners to build wealth through repayments, while renters face no such compulsion.
4. Tenant poverty and exposed groups. In the SOEP household panel, the share of tenants below 60 percent of median income, before housing costs, rose from about 16 percent in the early 1990s to just under 29 percent in 2015, while owners stayed near 4 percent. The authors count owners' saved rent as income and tie part of the rise in poverty risk across the whole population to newly arrived migrants. Among households aged 65 and over, 38 percent of tenants spent more than 40 percent of income on housing in 2016, against about a fifth in 1996. Students with their own household spent 54 percent of disposable income on housing in 2025, against 24 percent for the whole population, and 65 percent were overburdened. In big cities, households with a migration background lived on 34 square metres per person against 50 for others, yet paid a slightly higher share of income.
5. Cramped and cold. By the Eurostat definition, 11.7 percent of people in Germany lived in overcrowded homes in 2025, up from 10.2 percent in 2020, against 16.8 percent in the EU. The rate is 18.3 percent for market-rent tenants but under 4 percent for owners, 27.4 percent below the poverty line, and 46.7 percent for poor children. Sebastian Kohl and colleagues, funded by the Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, find that overcrowding has risen since 2012 and that urban tenants' floor space per person stagnated or fell, but that once children and migration background are controlled, economic factors explain relatively little. In 2025, 5.7 percent of people could not keep their home adequately warm, 12.6 percent below the poverty line, and 4.6 percent were in arrears on utility bills, 8.0 percent below it; these series do not split by tenure, so they show no direct link to rent.
6. Lock-in. Niklas Gohl asked whether tenants paying far below the market rent stay put. In SOEP data for 2012 to 2016, private tenants with a rent discount of at least 30 percent, living where rents rose more than 4 percent a year, were about 3 percentage points less likely to move than other private tenants, who moved about 10 percent of the time each year. The gap was wider for low-income tenants and for those who were dissatisfied or found the flat too small. With person-level fixed effects the main estimate falls to 1.7 points, and Gohl stresses that the design is not causal and the data do not show whether people wanted to move.
7. Displacement and segregation. Fabian Beran and Henning Nuissl surveyed more than 2,000 Berlin tenants who had recently moved: more than 15 percent had been directly displaced, most often through a rent increase after refurbishment or a sale (abstract only). Marcel Helbig and Stefanie Jähnen of the WZB Berlin Social Science Center studied 74 cities to 2014. The share of benefit recipients who would have had to move for an even spread across neighbourhoods rose from 24.0 percent in 2005 to 26.6 percent in 2014, and 36 cities have neighbourhoods where over half of the children live on such benefits. Yet higher average rents did not increase segregation. A federal study of twelve quarters in nine cities found displacement of older people and of people starting families, but also that student flat shares compete well, so a simple story of rich replacing poor is too narrow.
8. Social housing today. There is no official count of social rental flats. A Länder-based estimate puts them at 2.87 million in 1990 and 1.07 million in 2022, about 4.7 percent of rented homes. The rent and occupancy caps typically last 25 or 30 years, and holding the stock level would take about 41,200 new caps a year to 2035, against about 21,600 social rental flats built a year in 2018 to 2022. DIW Berlin's Konstantin Kholodilin and Pio Baake report that since 2002 the share of tenants spending over 40 percent of income on rent has exceeded the share living in social housing, and in 2021 it was almost twice as high. A comparison of up to 48 countries finds Germany's 76 percent fall from its peak the steepest in the West. Why the stock shrank belongs to the next episodes.
9. Wohngeld, the housing benefit. Wohngeld goes to lower-income households that do not receive basic income support. Its amount depends on household size, countable income and rent, rising with rent and falling with income, and rent counts only up to a ceiling set by the local rent level, one of seven Mietenstufen. The 2023 reform, Wohngeld-Plus, widened eligibility and added a heating-cost and a climate component. Recipient households rose 80 percent, from about 651,800 at the end of 2022 to about 1.17 million a year later, and reached about 1.3 million at the end of 2025, or 3.2 percent of households, at an average of 296 euros a month; in 51 percent the main earner is a pensioner. In 2024 fewer than 1 percent of recipient households lived in the highest rent level, which includes Munich, and about 70 percent in the lowest three. How many eligible households never claim is unsettled: a simulation for the federal institute BBSR found just under half before the reform, local offices guessed 17 percent, and an ifo paper cites a review giving 56 to 87 percent.
10. Basic income support and rent. Under Bürgergeld, the basic income support, "appropriate" housing costs are paid in full, and in the first twelve months the rent is not checked, as the Institute for Employment Research (IAB) described the rules in 2023. Where rent exceeds the local limit, households must cut costs, move or pay the difference from their standard allowance, unless a hardship exception applies; in a 2016 survey of local offices these covered 10.4 percent of households over the limit under SGB II, the system for jobseekers, and 34.4 percent under SGB XII, which covers older people and those unable to work. In the IAB's example of two fictional single people earning about 2,000 euros gross, roughly 1,150 euros remain after housing costs in Gera but about 900 in Munich, even with Wohngeld.

item.title: A1 · Can People Still Afford Rent? Then vs Now
item.description:
1. Three yardsticks, not one. The rent burden (Mietbelastung) is gross cold rent, meaning the basic rent plus the service charges paid to the landlord but not heating, as a share of household net income. Social scientists and property experts usually treat a burden above 30 percent as problematic, a rule of thumb rather than a measured boundary. The overburden rate used by Eurostat and the OECD counts people in households that spend more than 40 percent of disposable income on housing; in its wider version, housing costs also include utilities, maintenance and taxes. The third yardstick is residual income: what is left after housing costs, compared with the subsistence minimum. One research paper on German rent burdens puts it plainly: affordability cannot be measured directly, so rent-to-income ratios serve as a measurable indicator.
2. The official snapshot for 2022. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), tenant households spent on average 27.9 percent of their net income on gross cold rent, at 8.60 euros per square metre. In the first results, about 3.1 million households, 16 percent of tenant households, paid 40 percent or more. There is a catch for any "then versus now" question. Since the 2020 redesign of the Mikrozensus, the household survey behind these numbers, Destatis says 2022 cannot be compared with earlier years.
3. The long-run trend: up, then flat. Using the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), a household survey run since 1984, the DIW Berlin economists Konstantin Kholodilin and Pio Baake find that the burden rose in the early 1990s, has been roughly constant since about 2005, and has slipped slightly since 2015. In East Germany it jumped from about 4 percent in 1990 to about 25 percent in 2001, after rents frozen since 1936 were liberalised. Backhaus, Gebers and Schröder found the same shape: a substantial rise in the 1990s, then a relatively constant decade. Kholodilin and Baake name rising incomes, the rent brake (Mietpreisbremse, introduced in 2015 for new lettings in tight markets) and fewer moves as possible reasons for the recent slight fall, but say their data cannot show how much the brake mattered.
4. Rents against incomes. Asking rents, the rents advertised for new lettings, rose about 55 percent between 2010 and 2022, and about 70 percent in cities above 500,000 people. Rents in existing tenancies rose only about 19 percent. Over a shorter window, an Institut der deutschen Wirtschaft (IW) short report by Ralph Henger found that rents in multi-family buildings rose 10.2 percent from 2010 to 2016 while disposable household income rose 11.5 percent. Niklas Gohl, citing federal data, puts the rise for new contracts between 2010 and 2015 at about 18 percent nationally and 26 percent in big cities.
5. Sitting tenants versus newcomers. The federal research institute BBSR reports that in 2025 the average asking rent for a re-letting was 11.11 euros per square metre, against an estimated 7.76 euros for existing contracts: about 43 percent higher. Growth in asking rents slowed from 5.7 percent in 2023 to 4.8 and then 3.5 percent in 2024 and 2025. BBSR's explanation is that most flats are let long-term, and increases in running contracts are infrequent and legally limited. Gohl describes those limits as of 2019: a cap of 20 percent in three years, or 15 percent where states have designated tight markets. The size of the gap depends on the yardstick. BBSR's asking rents come from online adverts and its existing-rent figure is an estimate, while the IW found an average premium for new contracts of 14 percent in 2016 to 2018.
6. Newcomers: a third more per square metre, but a smaller gap in burden. In 2022 the average burden by move-in year was 26.9 percent before 1999, 27.3 percent for 1999 to 2008, 27.1 percent for 2009 to 2018, and 29.6 percent for 2019 or later. Recent movers pay 9.70 euros gross cold per square metre against 7.30 for pre-1999 tenants, about a third more, yet their burden is only about three points higher. The table does not say why. The IW reported that new tenants lived in somewhat less space per person than sitting tenants, 45.6 against 49.5 square metres in 2018.
7. Income is the sharpest divide. In 2022, households with under 1,500 euros net a month spent 44.6 percent of income on gross cold rent; households with 4,000 euros or more spent 15.9 percent. Households of four or more people under 1,500 euros spent 58.0 percent. Single-person households averaged 32.7 percent, two-person households 22.8 percent. Over time, Kholodilin and Baake find that the poorest fifth of tenants went from about 24 percent in 1990 to about 36 percent in 2021, while the richest fifth paid about 22 percent. Dustmann, Fitzenberger and Zimmermann, using a different survey and counting owners too, find that the bottom fifth's share of income spent on housing rose from 27 percent in 1993 to 39 percent in 2013, while the top fifth's fell from 16 to 14 percent.
8. Place matters, but less than income. In 2022 the burden was 29.0 percent in large cities, 27.7 percent in medium-sized towns and 26.0 percent in small towns and rural areas. Gross cold rent averaged 9.60 euros per square metre in large cities, and 11.00 euros for those who moved in from 2019. The burden for large-city newcomers was 30.9 percent. The spread by city size is far narrower than the spread by income. Asking rents in 2025 ranged from 21.01 euros in Munich to 8.64 in sparsely populated rural districts, and below 6 euros in parts of Saxony and Thuringia. Kholodilin and Baake find burdens lower in the East, with the statistical region of Chemnitz at 21.6 percent and the Cologne administrative district at 30.7 percent. The IW calculated, for new-contract rents, how much space a single median earner can rent for a quarter of net income: 36.2 square metres in Munich, 57.3 in Düsseldorf. Between 2018 and 2021, affordability fell in about three quarters of districts.
9. Germany in Europe: bad or good, depending on the yardstick. In 2025, 11.2 percent of Germany's population lived in households overburdened by housing costs, against 7.7 percent for the EU. The rate was 9.0 percent in 2020 and peaked at 13.0 percent in 2023; Destatis notes that figures from 2020 on are not comparable with earlier years because of a survey break, and that changed questions for owners in 2023 limit comparison with earlier years. Among people at risk of poverty the rate was 35.0 percent in 2025. Yet the OECD lists Germany among just five countries where fewer than half of low-income tenants in the private market are overburdened when total housing costs are counted. Germany also has the highest tenant share in the EU, with 52.8 percent of the population renting.
10. Residual income tells a related story. A Humboldt University team (Andrej Holm and colleagues), funded by the Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, used the 2018 Mikrozensus for 77 large cities. They found 12.9 percent of tenant households, about 1.1 million, had less than the subsistence minimum left after paying rent including utilities. The top income class had 4.4 times the net income of the bottom class before rent, and 6.7 times after it. A study of Berlin, Cologne and the Ruhr area from 2002 to 2018 by Marco Schmandt points the other way in aggregate: residual income rose along the whole distribution in two of the three markets despite real rent increases, largely because of changes in who lives there (abstract only).
